Under the hood

How Tumble Lab simulates the world

There's no Box2D, no matter.js, no WebAssembly. The whole engine is about 350 lines of vanilla JavaScript in js/engine.js. Here's exactly how it keeps hundreds of balls, ropes and cloth panels moving believably at 60 FPS.

1. Position-based Verlet integration

Most game engines store a position x and a velocity v. Tumble Lab stores a current position and a previous position instead. Velocity is never stored — it's implied by the gap between the two. This is position Verlet, and it's wonderfully stable: constraints that move a particle automatically change its velocity for free.

// velocity is implicit: v = x − xₚᵣₑᵥ vx = (x − prevX) * (1 − airFriction) vy = (y − prevY) * (1 − airFriction) prevX = x; prevY = y x += vx + gravityX · dt² y += vy + gravityY · dt²

2. Constraints: the glue for ropes & cloth

A rope is just a chain of particles joined by distance constraints. Each constraint has a rest length; if the two endpoints drift too far apart or too close, the constraint nudges them back along the line between them, splitting the correction by mass. Pinned particles have infinite mass, so they don't move — that's how a flag stays attached to its pole.

delta = b − a d = ‖delta‖ diff = (d − restLength) / d // move each end proportionally to its inverse mass a += delta · 0.5 · stiffness · diff b −= delta · 0.5 · stiffness · diff

One pass of constraint-solving doesn't fully satisfy every link at once — moving particle A to please one constraint can violate its neighbour. So the solver runs the whole list several times per frame (the Solver passes slider). More passes means a stiffer rope and a less stretchy cloth, at the cost of CPU.

3. Tearing

Each constraint can carry a tear ratio. When a thread is stretched beyond, say, 4× its rest length, it permanently breaks and stops solving. That single check is the entire "tearable cloth" feature — pull hard enough and the fabric rips along the weakest seam.

4. Collisions & the broadphase

Balls push each other apart when they overlap. Checking every pair would be O(n²) — slow for hundreds of bodies. Instead each frame builds a uniform spatial hash: the canvas is diced into cells, every particle is filed into its cell, and we only test a particle against bodies in its own cell and the eight neighbours.

overlap = (rₐ + r_b) − distance // push apart along the contact normal, weighted by inverse mass a -= normal · (invMassₐ / total) · overlap b += normal · (invMass_b / total) · overlap

5. Walls, restitution & friction

The canvas edges are hard walls. When a particle pokes through one, we snap it back to the boundary and reflect its implied velocity, scaled by the Bounciness (restitution) value. The tangential component is scaled down to fake surface friction, so balls eventually stop skidding and come to rest.

6. Rigid-ish boxes

A crate is four corner particles wired into a square — four edge constraints plus two diagonals. The diagonals are what stop it collapsing into a parallelogram, giving you a box that's rigid enough to stack but soft enough to crumple a little on a hard landing. It's a cheap trick that behaves remarkably like a real rigid body.

Accessibility & performance

  • Respects prefers-reduced-motion: trails off, fewer particles, starts paused.
  • Every control is keyboard reachable; the canvas is focusable and documents its shortcuts.
  • A fixed, clamped timestep keeps the simulation stable whether you run at 30 or 144 FPS.
  • Your last-used gravity, bounce, friction, spawn type and visuals are saved to localStorage.
